opus-5.5.text:
I think the core issue is a mismatch of incentives. A PhD student is evaluated mainly by papers. Your advisor, your committee, and the job market all look at what *you* contributed as a first author. Maintaining an existing open-source project is very different. Much of the work is invisible: reviewing other people's pull requests, fixing bugs, answering issues, keeping CI green, refactoring code so the next person can build on it. That work is extremely valuable for the community, but it rarely becomes a paper, and even when it does, the credit is shared among many people.

Timing matters too. When you join a project that is already successful, the "big ideas" that made it famous are already there and already credited to someone else. You come in and work on the second-order problems. These are often the hardest engineering problems, but from an academic point of view they look incremental. Many students reasonably ask themselves: "If I spend two years on this, what do I graduate with?"

Then there's the time horizon. A paper project has a deadline. You push hard, submit, and move on. Maintenance never ends. Being a core maintainer means you're on call. Users depend on you, and you have to respond when something breaks. That kind of long-term responsibility is hard to combine with the rhythm of a PhD, where you're also expected to explore, take courses, and switch topics.

Finally, it takes a particular personality. You need to enjoy engineering for its own sake and care about real users more than citations. You also have to be comfortable with the fact that your impact shows up in the form of "millions of people run this code" rather than "my h-index went up." Those people exist, but they're a minority among PhD students, and the ones who have that mindset often get attracted by industry offers before they ever commit to a project.

So it's not that PhD students lack the ability. Many of them are excellent engineers. The academic system just doesn't reward this kind of contribution well yet. For me personally, I was lucky. I found the work meaningful, and I believed that building infrastructure people actually use is itself a form of research impact. But I understand why it's a hard choice for most students.

r001.rationale: The response says PhD students are evaluated by papers and that maintaining a successful project often yields incremental, shared-credit work. It does not connect early-stage students’ publication needs to leading new projects.

r002.rationale: The response mentions the job market and industry offers, but does not say late-stage students have limited maintenance time because they are focused on finding jobs.

r003.rationale: The response does not identify middle- to later-stage PhD students as the best suited to maintain open-source projects.

fable-5.1.text:
Thanks for having me. I think the honest answer is that it comes down to incentives, and the incentives for a PhD student mostly point away from maintenance work.

A PhD student is evaluated on papers. Your advisor, your committee, your future employer, they all look at what you published and whether you were first author. Maintaining an existing project doesn't produce papers. If you write a new system from scratch, you can publish it. If you spend a year making vLLM's scheduler more robust, fixing distributed inference bugs, reviewing other people's pull requests, that's enormously valuable to users, but there's no venue that accepts "I kept this thing working." So the rational choice for a student is to build something new, even if it duplicates existing work, because novelty is what gets rewarded.

The second thing is that maintenance is mostly invisible labor. When a project works, nobody notices. When it breaks, everyone notices. So the feedback you get as a maintainer is skewed negative. You spend a lot of time on issues, on CI, on compatibility with new hardware and new models, and most of that is reactive rather than creative. For a student who is trying to form a research identity, that's a hard sell.

Third, there's a real ownership problem with an existing project. If you join something that's already large, you don't get to make the key design decisions. Those were made before you arrived. You inherit technical debt you didn't create, and you have to spend months just understanding the codebase before you can contribute meaningfully. Students have limited time, usually four or five years, and spending the first year reading code feels expensive.

And then there's the structural issue that open-source maintenance in machine learning has become very demanding. The pace is brutal. A new model architecture comes out every week, there are new attention variants, new quantization formats, new accelerators. Users expect support within days. That's a full-time job, and a PhD student is not supposed to have a full-time job on the side.

I was in a somewhat unusual position because my advisor was supportive and I could frame some of the engineering work as research, for example on compilation and system design. But I'd say that's the exception. Most students who contribute do so as a side project, and when the thesis pressure ramps up, they naturally leave. The ones who stay often end up in industry, where the incentives finally align, because companies actually depend on the software working.

So if we want students as core maintainers, I think the academic reward system has to change a little. Count maintainership as a contribution. Let a well-maintained system be part of a thesis. Otherwise we're asking people to act against their own interests, and that's not sustainable.

r001.rationale: The response says PhD students are rewarded for publishing and may choose to build new systems instead of maintaining existing ones, but it does not connect this incentive specifically to early-stage students.

r002.rationale: It says students may leave as thesis pressure rises and that industry incentives align, but does not attribute late-stage students’ limited maintenance time to job hunting.

r003.rationale: The response does not identify middle-to-late-stage PhD students as especially suited to maintenance.

astra-6.text:
I think the main reason is that the incentives are different. A PhD student needs to develop their own research direction and publish papers. But being a core maintainer of an existing project means spending a lot of time reviewing pull requests, fixing bugs, answering questions, and making sure changes don’t break things. That work is valuable, but it doesn’t necessarily turn into a research contribution.

There’s also the question of ownership. Students usually want something they can point to and say, “This is my contribution.” In an established project, you first have to understand decisions other people made, and then work within those constraints. You can spend months becoming useful without having a clear result for your thesis.

So I don’t think it’s a lack of interest in open source. It’s that the maintainer role has to fit their research goals. If working on the project helps them explore a research question and get recognition for their contribution, it becomes much more attractive.

r001.rationale: The response says PhD students need to develop research directions and publish, but does not specify early-stage students or say that publications favor leading new projects over maintaining existing ones.

r002.rationale: The response does not mention late-stage students’ job search or connect it to limited time for maintenance.

r003.rationale: The response does not identify middle- to later-stage PhD students as best suited to maintaining open-source projects.

I think the main challenge is that the incentives are different. As a PhD student, you need to develop your own research ideas and publish papers. But maintaining an existing open-source project means spending a lot of time reviewing pull requests, fixing bugs, answering questions, and keeping things working. Those contributions are valuable, but they don’t necessarily translate into a paper.

There’s also the question of ownership. A student usually wants a research direction they can call their own. Joining an established project means learning the existing codebase and working within decisions other people have made. So unless the maintenance work connects closely to their research, it’s difficult to make it their main priority.
